title: Business Communication Skills
summary: Learn to communicate clearly at work: principles of clear messages, professional emails, reports and proposals, effective meetings, presentations and feedback, and cross-cultural and digital communication.
audience: Students, employees, managers and entrepreneurs who want to communicate with impact

body.p: Business communication succeeds when the reader or listener understands quickly and knows what to do. Every message should answer three questions before you write it: who is the audience, what is the purpose, and what action or understanding do I want?

list: Clear: plain words, short sentences, one idea per paragraph.
Concise: cut words that add nothing; respect people's time.
Complete: include the facts, dates and amounts the reader needs to act.
Correct: check names, figures and spelling; errors damage credibility.
Courteous: polite and respectful, even when delivering bad news.

body.p: Time matters. A 1200-word email read at about 240 words a minute takes 5 minutes; sent to 50 people, it costs about 250 minutes of reading, more than 4 hours. A 300-word version takes about 1.25 minutes each.

body.tip: Before sending, ask, "If the reader only reads the first two lines, will they know what I need?"

body.p: Most workplace communication is written. Put the main point first (sometimes called BLUF: bottom line up front), then the details.

list: Subject line that says what it is about and what is needed: "Approval needed by Friday: Q3 training budget".
Opening sentence with the request or main point.
Short paragraphs or bullet points for details.
Specific action, owner and deadline.
Polite closing and your contact details.
Email: formal requests, records and messages for several people.
Instant messaging: quick questions and coordination; avoid long or sensitive discussions.
Phone or video call: complex, urgent or emotional issues.
Formal letter: legal, contractual or official matters.

body.p: Professional tone avoids slang, sarcasm and writing in capital letters. Messages can be forwarded, so never write anything you would not want the subject to read.

body.tip: Reply to all only when everyone needs the reply; unnecessary messages waste others' time.

body.p: Reports present information and recommendations; proposals persuade a reader to approve a plan or buy a service. Both should be easy to skim.

list: Title and date.
Executive summary: the key findings and recommendations in a few lines, written last.
Introduction: purpose and scope.
Findings: organised under clear headings, with tables or charts where they help.
Conclusions and recommendations: specific, practical and linked to the findings.
Appendices: detailed data and supporting material.
Start with the client's problem and goals, not your company history.
Explain the solution, timeline, responsibilities and price clearly.
Show evidence: past results, references and case studies.
State the benefits in the client's terms: money saved, risk reduced, time gained.
End with clear next steps.

body.tip: Use headings that say something: "Sales fell 12% in the Northern region" tells the reader more than "Regional sales".

body.p: Meetings are expensive. Eight people earning about R300 an hour in a 90-minute meeting cost 8 x 300 x 1.5 = R3600 in time, before preparation and travel. Hold a meeting only when discussion or decisions are needed; share updates in writing.

list: Before: set a clear purpose, invite only the people needed, and share an agenda with times and any reading in advance.
During: start on time, keep to the agenda, involve quieter people, and record decisions and actions as you go.
After: send brief minutes within a day listing decisions, actions, owners and deadlines.
Online: test technology, use video when possible, mute when not speaking, and make sure remote participants are heard.
Summarise discussions to check agreement.
Park off-topic issues in a list for later.
Ask for objections before closing a decision.
End on time; it builds trust in your meetings.

body.tip: Calculate the cost of your regular meetings once; it usually leads to shorter, fewer and better meetings.

body.p: Business presentations should lead with the message and recommendation, support it with a few strong points and evidence, and end with the action needed. Use slides as visual support: one idea per slide, large readable text and simple charts, not paragraphs to read aloud.

A simple model is situation, behaviour, impact (SBI): "In yesterday's client meeting (situation), you interrupted the client twice (behaviour), and she stopped sharing her concerns (impact)." Then discuss what to do differently. Describe specific behaviour, not personality, and give feedback soon, privately for criticism.

list: Listen without defending yourself immediately.
Ask questions to understand examples.
Thank the person, even if you disagree.
Decide what to act on and follow up.

body.p: Prepare the key message, choose a private setting, state the issue directly but kindly, listen to the other person's view, and agree next steps. Avoiding hard conversations usually lets problems grow.

body.tip: Practise a presentation aloud at least twice, timed; most people run long.

body.p: Teams and customers increasingly span countries, languages and cultures. Cultures differ in how direct people are, how hierarchy is shown, how time and deadlines are treated, and how much context is left unsaid.

list: Use simple, clear English and avoid idioms and slang that translate badly.
Check understanding by asking people to summarise, not just "Do you understand?"
Learn local greetings, titles and meeting customs.
Be patient and curious rather than judgemental about differences.
Confirm important agreements in writing.
Keep professional profiles accurate and respectful.
Think before posting: content is permanent and searchable.
Protect confidential and personal information, as data-protection laws require.
Respect time zones and working hours when messaging colleagues.
Use accessible formats: readable fonts, alt text for images, captions for videos.

body.tip: When a written message could be misread, add a short friendly line or pick up the phone; tone is easily lost in text.

quiz.q: Which three questions should you answer before writing a message?
options: What font, what colour, what size?
Who is the audience, what is the purpose, what action is wanted?
How long, how many, how late?
Who is the boss, who is absent, who is new?

quiz.q: A 1200-word email read at 240 words a minute takes:
Sent to 50 people, how much total reading time is that?

options: Put the bottom line up front
Approval needed by Friday: Q3 training budget

quiz.q: Which channel suits a sensitive, emotional issue?
options: A phone or video call (or in person)

quiz.q: When is a report's executive summary usually written?
8 people at R300 an hour in a 90-minute meeting cost about:
In the SBI feedback model, the B stands for:
When receiving feedback you should first:
Why avoid idioms with international colleagues?
How should you check understanding across cultures?
options: Ask people to summarise the key points
